title: Lawmakers Propose 20%-30% U.S. Film Tax Incentive to Revive Hollywood Production】
body:
Washington – A bipartisan coalition of lawmakers introduced a sweeping bill on Thursday that would establish a federal film‑production tax credit ranging from 20 percent to 30 percent, aiming to revive U.S. studio activity that has been drifting overseas for years. The legislation, dubbed the “American Film Production Incentive Act,” seeks to make the United States the most attractive destination for high‑budget movies and television series by offering a stackable, refundable credit that can be combined with existing state‑level incentives. Proponents argue the measure could generate billions in economic activity, protect thousands of jobs, and reassert Hollywood’s global leadership in storytelling.

The proposed credit would be “stackable,” meaning producers could layer the federal incentive on top of state tax credits that already exist in many film‑friendly jurisdictions such as Georgia, New Mexico, and Louisiana. By allowing a combined discount of up to 30 percent of qualified production expenditures, the bill hopes to counteract the aggressive subsidies offered by countries like Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia, which have lured a growing share of U.S. projects abroad. The legislation also includes provisions for a “regional multiplier” that would give additional credit points to productions that film in historically under‑served areas, thereby spreading economic benefits beyond the traditional hubs of Los Angeles and New York.

Supporters in Congress, led by Representatives Anna Lee (D‑CA) and Michael Torres (R‑TX), framed the incentive as a national‑security issue for the cultural sector. “Our stories are part of America’s soft power,” Lee said during a press briefing. “When we lose productions to foreign tax breaks, we lose jobs, tax revenue, and the ability to shape the global narrative.” Torres added that the bill would create a “level playing field” for American studios competing with foreign competitors that already enjoy generous subsidies. The bipartisan nature of the effort reflects growing concern across party lines that the U.S. film industry’s decline could have broader economic repercussions, especially in states that rely heavily on production spending for local employment.

Critics, however, warn that a large federal credit could strain the Treasury and set a precedent for other industries to demand similar subsidies. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that the program could cost the federal government between $2 billion and $4 billion annually, depending on uptake. Fiscal conservatives argue that the incentive may simply shift production from one state to another without creating net new activity, a phenomenon known as “cannibalization.” Moreover, some industry analysts point out that the rise of streaming platforms has already altered the economics of content creation, reducing the relative importance of location‑based tax breaks.

The bill also touches on broader policy debates about the role of government in the creative economy. While state governments have long used tax credits to attract film work, a federal counterpart would standardize the playing field and potentially reduce the “race to the bottom” where states compete by offering ever‑larger rebates. Yet, the legislation includes safeguards: credits would be refundable only after a production meets a minimum spend threshold, and a portion of the credit would be earmarked for hiring local talent and crew, aiming to bolster workforce development in the industry.

If passed, the American Film Production Incentive Act could reshape the geography of U.S. entertainment production within the next two to three years. Studios that have already begun relocating parts of their pipelines to Canada and Europe might reconsider, especially for mid‑budget projects where a 20‑30 percent tax credit could make the difference between filming domestically or abroad. Lawmakers are expected to move the bill to committee hearings in the coming weeks, where industry stakeholders will have the opportunity to testify. As the debate unfolds, the entertainment sector watches closely, aware that the outcome could determine whether Hollywood retains its pre‑eminence or cedes ground to a new generation of global production hubs.
